name: Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time
problem: A model's memory is either its finite context window (short-term) or its weights (fixed at training time); there is no mechanism that ACQUIRES and retains new information at inference the way a cache does.
mechanism: Neural memory: a long-term persistent memory module with three variants differing in how it is written and read - persistent memory as a straightforward long-term memory; momentum update; and surprise-based (gradient-like) update. This memory is combined with short-term memory as attention and, in the data-dependence variant, a context-based gating decides per input whether to query the long-term memory.
speedup_reported: NOT A THROUGHPUT CLAIM. The abstract reports quality: more effective than Transformers and recent modern linear recurrent models on language modelling, common-sense reasoning, genomics and time series; and scaling to LARGER THAN 2M context window with higher needle-in-a-haystack accuracy than baselines. The 2M context figure is a capability result with no baseline engine or memory footprint attached.

  mechanism: the retired record's text was materially fuller (844 chars vs 407) and is RETAINED here rather than discarded. Its text: Proposes a neural long-term memory module, framed explicitly as learning to memorise at TEST TIME: a surprising-as-written design where memory is a persistent, weights-derived long-term memory rather than something computed by a forward pass over the sequence. As a recurrent/persistent module it maintains its own memory matrices across a very long window, using momentum-style updates to decide what to write and a surprise measure (a test-time loss) to decide what to retrieve, and it is combined with attention so attention handles the current local context while the module supplies long past information. The memory is a set of persistent matrices with a fixed, budgeted size (the paper explores different memory sizes as a scaling axis), so memory capacity is a design parameter independent of context length rather than growing with it.
